newsitem.title: USA: U.S. criticizes EU challenge to Cuba trade law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. criticizes EU challenge to Cuba trade law.

text.p: The European Union should work with the United States to bring democracy to Cuba instead of challenging an anti-Cuba trade law, U.S. officials said on Tuesday.

Charlene Barshefsky, the acting U.S. trade representative, said a decision by foreign ministers to challenge the so-called Helms-Burton law "unnecessarily escalates tensions." EU officials said a complaint would be lodged with the World Trade Organisation on Oct. 16.

The Helms-Burton law brought strong protests from other nations because it allowed lawsuits against foreign investors who profited from property seized from Americans after the 1959 revolution. A number of nations prepared "antidote" laws to override the U.S. law.
President Bill Clinton suspended the section allowing lawsuits but said international cooperation against Cuba would be a factor when he decided in January whether to suspend the provision again.
"Our position is very clear. The law is absolutely consistent with our international obligations. We intend to defend it," Barshefsky told reporters.
"In our view, what is needed is action by our allies to promote democracy in Cuba."
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns called the EU decision "unfortunate" and a disappointment.
"We would have vastly preferred a bilateral, if you will, EU-U.S. solution to this and continued dialogue," Burns said.
Commerce Undersecretary Stuart Eizenstat, acting as a special envoy, met leaders of several nations during September to try to win support for coordinated action against Cuba.
"We believe that Helms-Burton should continue to be discussed between friends and that unilateral action should not be taken," Burns said.
Barshefsky said the administration sought through implementation of the Helms-Burton law to maximize pressure on Cuba while minimising frictions with trading partners.

The United States has barred more than a dozen executives from a Canadian mining firm and a Mexican telecommunications company from visiting the country because of their involvement with business in Cuba.
